prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for showing how exporting, foreign investment and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B001 alone, credited to Helpman and Melitz. My reasons are the ones I gave in round 1, tested against the exchange. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) give a single, identifiable mechanism: productivity differences across firms drive selection into exporting and foreign investment, and trade reallocates activity toward more productive firms. The mechanism produced sharp predictions, and those predictions have been checked in firm-level data from many countries for more than two decades. Where baseline predictions fail in detail, the model has been extended rather than dropped. From a metascience viewpoint, that is what a credible research programme looks like: a clear core result, repeated independent testing and a durable change in practice. The chair's summary shows that all eleven round-1 files prefer this configuration. I do not count that as evidence of merit, and I note the chair's caveat that agreement among instances of one model may reflect shared reasoning patterns. So I used round 2 to look for the strongest objections, not to confirm the count. The two serious ones are the omitted Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum lineage and the sensitivity of the welfare magnitudes to distributional assumptions. I think both can be handled by a narrow citation, which now says selection and reallocation and makes no claim about the size of the gains. I changed one thing: my alternatives are now B006 and B030, and B035 drops out. The cap is two, and the exchange gave me much more evidence on B006 than on B035. Nothing in the exchange lowered my view of B035's merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution at the edges. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related, partly parallel contributions, on exporter premia and on Ricardian heterogeneity, and none is on this ballot entry. If the Committee reads the discovery as the empirical facts plus the theory, a two-name award is arguably too narrow, and I cannot cure that by adding names the entry does not credit. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is substantial and is also left out. Second, the baseline model's welfare conclusions depend on functional-form and distributional assumptions, so the qualitative selection and reallocation predictions are more robust than the magnitudes. Third, Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work sits near the lineage recognised in 2008, and a member could reasonably judge the incremental step smaller than I do. I think these concerns are real but do not outweigh the core case. They do argue for a citation that stays within what the evidence supports.

responses.point: Enflo says she is less comfortable than some colleagues treating Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as only a caveat. If the Committee reads the discovery as the empirical facts plus the theory, the credited names would be incomplete. She answers that the prize recognises the model that organised those facts and created a new welfare channel, and she acknowledges this is a judgment about what counts as the discovery.
responses.response: I agree that this is a judgment about the unit of discovery, and the record cannot settle it. The test I would apply is the one I use for any claim. Which contribution generated a distinctive, falsifiable implication that others then tested? The exporter-premia facts preceded and motivated the theory. The selection mechanism and the exports-versus-FDI sorting result are what turned them into testable predictions about who exports, who invests abroad and where the reallocation gains come from. That supports crediting the model. It does not make the empirical lineage unimportant, and I would not want the citation or the background to imply it was. I would therefore say in the background that the empirical facts motivated the framework, and keep the citation on the framework. If a majority instead defines the discovery as the whole firm-level trade programme, I would accept that the ballot entry is too narrow and that this changes the comparison. I do not read the evidence in the files that way.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B006 first in the opening to B001 first in round 1, citing the sharper discovery boundary and cleaner attribution of B001. He keeps B006 as his first alternative. He also notes that the five credited people across B001 and B006 exceed the three-person limit, and that trimming to Pakes alone would fragment the BLP credit.
responses.response: This answers the chair's question on a two-part configuration for me. B001 uses two of the three places, so a second part could carry only one person. Under B006 that would be Pakes alone, which would split a credit that members describe as a Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core, and I would not support it. I therefore keep a single-part prize. I also take your point that B006 deserves to be a real fallback and not a courtesy. In round 1 I put the bar at out-of-sample validation, for example merger retrospectives, and at a bounded discovery. I said I would reconsider if B006 were narrowed to the demand-estimation core of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Since you and others treat that core as cleanly attributable and fully mature, I now list B006 as an alternative, with that narrowing as a condition. My remaining doubt is evidentiary and unchanged. Structural conclusions rest on instrument and functional-form assumptions, and the files give no systematic out-of-sample evidence either way. I have not verified this independently.

responses.point: Teorell weighs B001 against B006 on two grounds: B006 bundles demand estimation, dynamic games and entry models across seven names, and B001 changed the economic content of trade theory (who exports, who gains) as well as the toolkit. He also notes that Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work sits close to the lineage recognised in 2008, so part of the credit could be seen as already covered.
responses.response: I share your discovery-boundary point and use it as a metascience criterion. A prize should reward something that can be stated in one sentence and whose predictions can fail. B001 meets that standard better than the bundled B006 entry. On the 2008 overlap, I read Helpman's earlier work as foundation for the HMY step and not as the object of this award. That is a reason to write the citation around selection and exports-versus-FDI sorting, which is what I have done, and it does not make the credit duplicative. I would not rely on that distinction more than the files support, though. If a member thinks the incremental step over 2008 is too small, that is a legitimate scientific disagreement, and I would want it argued on the content and not on the timing of the field's last prize.

responses.point: Fredriksson keeps B001 first and wants the citation to stay narrow, naming selection and reallocation, because the baseline model is rejected in some details and its welfare conclusions rest on auxiliary distributional assumptions. He keeps B030 as an alternative and prefers Autor, Hanson and Katz, with the Katz-versus-Dorn caveat stated openly.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and have kept to that wording. It avoids implying that the size of the gains from trade is settled. On B030 I differ slightly on names. Katz's skill-demand work is shared with a 2023 laureate, so adding him blurs the boundary. I would define a B030 fallback narrowly around the trade-shock evidence, credited to Autor and Hanson as in my opening. I keep it second among my alternatives for two reasons. The persistence and interpretation of the China-shock effects are still debated, and the task framework has originators outside the credited names. The chair's question on whether the technology and trade strands are one discovery or two is therefore unresolved for me, and I would not merge them.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee defines the discovery as the selection and reallocation framework (Helpman, Melitz) or as the broader firm-level and quantitative trade programme. If it chooses the latter, the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on this entry, and Redding's claim would weigh more.
How much of the welfare and gains-from-trade conclusion survives relaxing the baseline model's distributional assumptions. I have therefore kept the citation on mechanism and not on magnitudes.

Whether B006 can be bounded to a coherent demand-estimation core (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes), and how much out-of-sample validation exists for structural IO methods. This decides whether it is a stronger fallback than I currently judge.
Whether the B030 trade-shock evidence can be separated from the task framework and from the 2023 and 2024 prizes, and how persistent the trade-shock effects are.
Convergence among the eleven round-1 files may partly reflect shared reasoning patterns in the simulation and not independent scientific judgment, so I cannot treat the agreement as confirmation.
I rely on the supplied files and general knowledge, and I have not independently verified citations, priority records or award histories.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Helpman, Melitz or any other credited name on B001, B006 or B030 is apparent from my supplied profile. My listed ties are the Institute for Replication (led by Abel Brodeur), the Harvard evolutionary-dynamics network (Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak), frequent co-authors such as Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber and Nosek, and SSE colleagues including Magnus Johannesson and Tore Ellingsen. None is a candidate on the shortlist. I note that Friberg co-authored with Ellingsen and that Andersson reports an SSE affiliation shared with me. I also disclose that my metascience background may lead me to weight robustness and replication evidence more heavily than colleagues do. That could bias me against B006 and toward B001. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
